2027-07-19.title: Third Monday of Kaitha
2027-07-19.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: Faith is brought to completion by works
2027-07-19.alt: Season of Kaitha (Qaita, Summer), which began on Sunday 4 July with the Feast of the Twelve Apostles: the season of the Church's growth and harvest, when the Church remembers the apostles and martyrs who watered her field with their blood and keeps herself ready for the coming of the Lord. The calendar's own headings: “Faith accomplished through the deeds”; “Jesus mourns over Jerusalem”.
2027-07-19.verse: For just as the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is also dead.
theo: The Season of Kaitha is the season of the harvest, and a harvest is judged by its fruit. Today's Epistle asks what the fruit of faith is. James places two very different people side by side: Abraham, the father of believers, and Rahab, a woman of Jericho whom the Bible calls a prostitute. “Was not our ancestor Abraham justified by works when he offered his son Isaac on the altar? You see that faith was active along with his works, and faith was brought to completion by the works.” James is not contradicting Paul. Paul argues against those who thought they could earn God's favour by keeping the Law; James argues against those who thought that a belief held in the head, with a closed hand and a closed door, is enough. Both of them quote the same verse, “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Genesis 15:6), and both know that faith is God's gift. But a gift received is a gift used. Abraham believed long before he climbed the mountain of Moriah; the climb was his faith made visible, and in that obedience, says James, faith “was brought to completion”. The Church teaches the same: faith is the beginning of salvation, and a faith that is not alive in hope and love does not unite us fully to Christ.

Then James names Rahab: “Likewise, was not Rahab the prostitute also justified by works when she welcomed the messengers and sent them out by another road?” Her story is told in the Book of Joshua. Two spies come to Jericho; she hides them on her roof, confesses that “The Lord your God is indeed God in heaven above and on earth below” (Joshua 2:11), and asks that her family be spared. Her faith did not stay in words: she risked her life and her house. The Letter to the Hebrews also names her among the people of faith (11:31), and Matthew places her in the family line of the Messiah (Matthew 1:5). So the patriarch and the foreigner, the greatest and the least, are justified in the same way, by a living faith that opens the door. James closes with the sentence that gathers the whole passage: “For just as the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is also dead.”

The Gospel takes us to the last teaching of Jesus in the Temple, after the seven woes. He speaks as a prophet of Israel who loves his people as only one of them could. “Therefore I send you prophets, sages, and scribes, some of whom you will kill and crucify, and some you will flog in your synagogues and pursue from town to town.” He points back over the whole long history of faithful witnesses, “from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah son of Barachiah”, from the first righteous man killed in Genesis to the last in the order of the Hebrew Scriptures (2 Chronicles 24:20–21). The prophets whom he now sends are the apostles and martyrs whom Kaitha honours. These hard words are to be read as the Church reads them: as a warning to every generation, ours included, and not as a verdict on a people. The Church teaches that the Jewish people as a whole are not to be blamed for the death of the Lord (Catechism 597–598), and that God's call to them is irrevocable (Romans 11:29). Jesus, his mother and his first disciples were all Jews.

Then the tone turns from warning to tenderness: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, the city that kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to it! How often have I desired to gather your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing!” Every Kerala household knows the picture: at the first shadow of a kite in the sky the mother hen spreads her wings and the chicks run under them. The psalmist already said of God, “he will cover you with his pinions, and under his wings you will find refuge” (Psalm 91:4). It is not God who is unwilling; “you were not willing”. His love never forces. Yet the lament ends with a promise: “you will not see me again until you say, ‘Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord.’” The words are from Psalm 118:26, which the crowds sing on Palm Sunday and which the Church repeats in the Sanctus of the Holy Qurbana. So we ask two questions today: what fruit does my faith bear, and have I let myself be gathered under his wings?
outline: A tree is known by its fruit: what does my faith look like on an ordinary Monday?
Abraham believed first and obeyed after; faith and works belong together.
Point 2 · The open door of Rahab
A stranger's living faith: welcome, risk and rescue.
The grief and tenderness of Jesus over Jerusalem; love that does not force.
live: Choose one concrete act this week that your faith asks of you: a visit, a bill paid on time, a quarrel ended, a gift to someone in need. Do it quietly.
Each evening this week, before sleep, say: “Lord, gather me under your wings,” and then name the people you want him to gather too.
fathers: Because of her faith and her hospitality Rahab the prostitute was saved. She received the spies and sent them out another way, and so she became a sign that those who trust in the Lord find redemption.
When the Lord says “How often”, he shows not anger but a love wounded by refusal. These are the words of one who grieves over a city he would have saved, not of one who hates it.
magis: The gift of faith remains in one who has not sinned against it. But faith without works is dead: when it is deprived of hope and love, it does not fully unite the believer to Christ or make him a living member of his Body.
It is not possible to lay responsibility for the Lord's Passion on the Jewish people as a whole. The Church sees the sins of all sinners as the cause of the sufferings of Christ.
The Jewish people are the first to have heard the Word of God; theirs is the covenant and the promises, and God's gifts and call to them are irrevocable.
saints: Third Monday of Kaitha. In Kerala the monsoon is at its height and the fields are green: a good day to remember that faith, like a crop, is known by its fruit.

19–24 July: the third week of Kaitha. Mon 19 to Wed 21 and Sat 24: the Third Week of Kaitha, with the Epistle from the Letter of James (Mon, Tue, Thu, Sat). Thu 22: Saint Mary Magdalene, apostle of the apostles, with readings of her own. Fri 23: the Third Friday of Kaitha (readings from the 2022–23 calendar, verify locally). Sat 24: in the Latin and Malankara calendars, Saint Sharbel Makhluf, a monk of the Maronite Church. Looking ahead: the Fourth Sunday of Kaitha on 25 July, and Saint Alphonsa on Wednesday 28 July.
2027-07-19.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you gathered your people under your wings, though they were not willing. Gather us today. Make our faith alive, like the faith of Abraham who obeyed and of Rahab who opened her door; let our hands do what our lips confess. Keep us from judging any people as you alone can judge, and teach us to grieve over the world as you grieved over Jerusalem. Welcome us when we come in your name, for you are blessed, you who come in the name of the Lord, now and for ever. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbana the Lord gathers his scattered children as a hen gathers her brood, around one altar, one bread and one cup. We come with the faith we confess in the Creed, and we are sent out to give it flesh in works of mercy, so that the Body we receive may live in the world through us.

quick: James: Abraham's faith was brought to completion by his obedience; Rahab's welcome of the messengers shows faith at work; faith without works is dead.
Matthew: Jesus sends prophets and wise men and scribes, warns of the cost of refusing them, and laments over Jerusalem like a hen who would gather her chicks.
Together: a living faith is a faith that obeys and welcomes, and the Lord is always the one who gathers.
2027-07-19.action: Do one act of faith this week that costs you something: a visit, a gift, a pardon.
2027-07-19.question: What fruit does my faith bear, and where have I been unwilling to be gathered?

family.explain: Rahab opened her door to two strangers and helped them, and God remembered her kindness. James tells us that believing in God and doing good go together, like a body and its breath. Jesus said he wanted to gather the people of Jerusalem like a mother hen gathers her chicks under her wings. Think of the chicks hurrying under the hen when a kite flies over: that is how safe we are with Jesus.
family.intention: We thank God for the people who sheltered us when we were small, and we pray for the lonely and for strangers who need a door opened.
family.ask: Ask: “Whose door can our family open this week, and how?”

illus: In a village near Kottayam (a story told to illustrate the reading) an old woman was known for saying her rosary on the front verandah every evening. One monsoon night the river rose and the poor house across the lane filled with water. She put down her beads, took a lantern, and went out into the rain with her grandsons; they carried the neighbours' mats and pots to her own verandah, and the family slept in her kitchen for a week. When the parish priest thanked her, she smiled and said, ‘The rosary brought me as far as the door. Then the door had to open.’

pm.open: Lord Jesus, you would gather us as a hen gathers her chicks. We come under your wings. Open our eyes to see what our faith asks of us today. Amen.
share: Abraham's faith was brought to completion by his works (James 2:22). Where is my faith still only in words?
Rahab welcomed the messengers (James 2:25). Whom could I welcome who is a stranger to me?
How often have I desired to gather your children (Matthew 23:37). When have I felt the Lord gathering me and I was unwilling?
You will not see me again until you say, Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord (Matthew 23:39). How do I welcome the Lord when he comes in the poor and the stranger?
pm.resp: Lord, gather us under your wings.
interc: For the Church, that her faith may be seen in works of mercy.
For the Jewish people, our elder brothers and sisters in faith, that God who called them will keep faith with them, and for peace between all peoples.
For those who have no home or shelter in this monsoon season.
For those whose faith has grown cold, that they may feel the Lord gathering them.
For ourselves, that our faith may bear fruit in good works.
pm.close: Father, you gather your children in Christ and ask for the obedience of faith. Make us alive in faith and generous in works, until we are gathered at last into your house. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, today's Epistle asks a simple question: what is your faith worth if nobody can see it? Saint James says: “For just as the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is also dead” (James 2:26).

He gives two examples. Abraham believed God, and then he obeyed God even when it was very hard. Rahab was a stranger in Jericho, yet she believed in the God of Israel and she risked her life to save two messengers. Both were justified; both had a faith that acted.

We are saved by the grace of God that we receive in faith, and that faith is alive when it shows itself in love. The believer does not earn God's love, but the one who has received it cannot keep it locked inside.

In the Gospel Jesus grieves over Jerusalem: “How often have I desired to gather your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing!” (Matthew 23:37). We know this picture from our own courtyards. Jesus is the one who would gather us; all that is asked of us is to be willing.
This week let us ask: where is my faith only words? Let us do one good deed that costs us something, and let us run under the Lord's wings each evening. Amen.
kids: Children, have you seen a mother hen when a kite flies over? She spreads her wings and all the chicks hurry underneath. Jesus said he wants to gather us like that, and be our safe place. And what do we do? We can run to him in prayer, and we can open the door to someone who needs help, like Rahab. That is faith that works!

intro: Theme: “For just as the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is also dead.”
A faith brought to completion by obedience, a stranger's open door, and the Lord who would gather us under his wings.

sub: The mountain of Moriah made his faith visible.
Faith is a gift; a gift is meant to be used.
q: And he believed the Lord; and the Lord reckoned it to him as righteousness.
You see that faith was active along with his works, and faith was brought to completion by the works.
points.apply: Choose one act this week through which your faith will be seen.

sub: She risked her life and her house.
The least and the greatest justified alike.
q: But Rahab the prostitute, with her family and all who belonged to her, Joshua spared. Her family has lived in Israel ever since. For she hid the messengers whom Joshua sent to spy out Jericho.
By faith Rahab the prostitute did not perish with those who were disobedient, because she had received the spies in peace.
points.apply: Open your door, your table or your time to one person who is a stranger to you.

sub: The grief of Jesus over Jerusalem.
Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord.
q: he will cover you with his pinions, and under his wings you will find refuge; his faithfulness is a shield and buckler.
How often have I desired to gather your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing!
points.apply: Each evening this week, ask the Lord to gather you and the people you love under his wings.

concl: Faith is a gift of God, and it is alive when it opens the hand and the door.
The Lord is always the one who gathers; our part is to be willing.
2027-07-19.resolve: This week, do one act that shows your faith, open a door to a stranger, and run to the Lord's wings each evening.
